subject: science
passage: Carl Linnaeus is remembered for the two-word scientific name, yet he did not set out to invent it. In Species Plantarum, published in 1753, the proper name of each plant was still a descriptive phrase of up to a dozen Latin words, and the two-word form appeared only in the margin, as a shorthand added for the convenience of indexing. Linnaeus regarded this shorthand as a mere label for ready reference, and he continued to treat the full phrase as the true name of the species. ______ it was the shorthand that endured: within a few decades naturalists across Europe had abandoned the phrase names altogether, and the marginal convenience had become the foundation of biological naming.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

explanation.why: The third sentence says Linnaeus treated the two-word name as a mere label and the phrase as the real name. The last sentence says that, contrary to his own view, the label is what survived. The transition must signal an outcome that occurred in spite of Linnaeus's intention.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The last sentence does not restate Linnaeus's view in other terms; it describes the opposite outcome.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Instead" would require a rejected action that something else replaced, but Linnaeus did not reject or abandon anything; the outcome simply ran against his view. This is the closest near miss.
explanation.C: Correct. "Nevertheless" signals that the shorthand endured even though Linnaeus himself regarded the phrase as the real name.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The survival of the shorthand was not a consequence of Linnaeus treating the phrase as the true name; it happened despite that.
